chapter.name: A Square and a Cube
chapter.blurb: Square numbers and their digit patterns, square roots, the prime-factorisation test for perfect squares, cubic numbers and cube roots.

scope_in.item: Square notation n squared as the area of a square of side n, and perfect squares as the squares of natural numbers
Squares of fractions and decimals, e.g. (3/5) squared = 9/25 and 2.5 squared = 6.25
The units digit of a perfect square is always 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9, never 2, 3, 7 or 8
A perfect square ends in an even number of zeros; the parity of a number and of its square agree
Consecutive odd numbers starting from 1 sum to consecutive perfect squares, and the test for a perfect square that follows from it
The sum of two consecutive triangular numbers is a perfect square
Square root as the inverse of squaring; every perfect square has one positive and one negative integer root; only the positive root is used in this chapter
Deciding whether a number is a perfect square, and finding its root, by splitting its prime factorisation into two identical groups
Estimating a square root by bracketing between known squares and using the units digit
Cubes as a number multiplied by itself three times, and perfect cubes 1, 8, 27, ...
Blocks of consecutive odd numbers summing to consecutive perfect cubes
Cube root notation, and the test for a perfect cube by splitting the prime factorisation into three identical groups

scope_out.item: Square roots of non-perfect squares as irrational numbers, and surds
scope_out.reason: Irrational numbers are a Class 9 topic; this chapter stays with perfect squares

scope_out.item: The long-division method for square roots
scope_out.reason: Not used anywhere in this chapter; roots are found by factorisation or estimation
Outside the number system used at this level

scope_out.item: Laws of exponents and powers beyond squares and cubes
scope_out.reason: A separate chapter; only index 2 and 3 appear here

scope_out.item: Surface area and volume formulas of a cube
scope_out.reason: The cube appears here as a number pattern, not as a solid to measure

concepts.name: Square numbers and perfect squares
concepts.description: A number multiplied by itself, written n squared, and the perfect squares that result when n is a natural number.
concepts.idea: The area of a square of side n is n by n, which is why n multiplied by itself is called 'n squared'.
concepts.rule: For any number n, n multiplied by n is written as n squared. The squares of the natural numbers 1, 2, 3, ... are called perfect squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...
concepts.example: A square of side 5 cm has area 5 x 5 = 5 squared = 25 sq. cm, so 25 is a perfect square.

concepts.name: Digit patterns and properties of perfect squares
concepts.description: What the units digit, the trailing zeros and the parity of a perfect square can and cannot be.
concepts.idea: Squaring cannot produce just any number: the last digit of a square is fixed by the last digit of the number squared.
concepts.rule: A perfect square ends in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9, never in 2, 3, 7 or 8. It ends in an even number of zeros. A number and its square have the same parity.
concepts.example: 327 ends in 7, so it cannot be a perfect square. 2800 ends in two zeros but 28 is not a square, so the digit test alone is not enough.

concepts.name: Perfect squares as sums of consecutive odd numbers
concepts.description: Adding consecutive odd numbers starting from 1 produces the perfect squares in order, and the test for a perfect square that follows.
concepts.idea: The gap between one square and the next grows by 2 each time: 4 - 1 = 3, 9 - 4 = 5, 16 - 9 = 7.
concepts.rule: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared. A natural number that cannot be written as such a sum is not a perfect square.
concepts.example: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4 squared, so 16 is the sum of the first 4 odd numbers.

concepts.name: Square roots
concepts.description: The inverse of squaring, the two integer roots of a perfect square, and the convention of taking the positive root.
concepts.idea: If the area of a square is known, its side is the square root of that area.
concepts.rule: If y = x squared then x is a square root of y. Every perfect square has one positive and one negative integer root; the symbol for the positive root is the radical sign.
concepts.example: A square of area 49 sq. cm has side 7 cm, so the square root of 49 is 7 (and -7 is the other root).

concepts.name: Testing for a perfect square by prime factorisation
concepts.description: Splitting a prime factorisation into two identical groups to decide whether a number is a perfect square and to read off its root.
concepts.idea: A square is a number multiplied by itself, so its prime factors must divide into two matching halves.
concepts.rule: If the prime factors of a number can be split into two identical groups, it is a perfect square and the product of one group is its square root. If any prime is left unpaired, it is not.
concepts.example: 324 = (2 x 3 x 3) x (2 x 3 x 3) = 18 squared, so the square root of 324 is 18. 156 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 13 leaves 3 and 13 unpaired, so 156 is not a perfect square.

concepts.name: Cubes and cube roots
concepts.description: Perfect cubes, the blocks of consecutive odd numbers that build them, cube-root notation and the three-identical-groups test.
concepts.idea: A cube of side n is built from n cubed unit cubes, just as a square of side n has area n squared.
concepts.rule: A number multiplied by itself three times is a cube. If y = x cubed then x is the cube root of y. A number is a perfect cube if its prime factors split into three identical groups.
concepts.example: 3375 = (3 x 5) x (3 x 5) x (3 x 5) = 15 cubed, so the cube root of 3375 is 15.

questions.q: The block 21 + 23 + 25 + 27 + 29 adds to 125. Explain how this fits the pattern of cubes, and predict how many odd numbers the next block will contain.
questions.a: 125 is 5 cubed, and the block contains exactly 5 consecutive odd numbers, matching the pattern that the nth block of n odd numbers adds to n cubed. The next block will contain 6 odd numbers and add to 216.

questions.q: A student says that the cube root of 27 is 9. Explain the mistake and give the correct value.
questions.a: The student divided 27 by 3 instead of finding the number that multiplies by itself three times. The cube root of 27 is 3, because 3 x 3 x 3 = 27.

Gives the correct cube root 3 with a check
